Family Health

Psoriasis around the anus: getting the right care

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Psoriasis can affect the skin around the anus as well as the genitals, groin and crease between the buttocks. In these moist, rubbing areas it may look smooth rather than covered in the familiar thick scales. It can be uncomfortable and difficult to discuss, but effective help is available. New anal symptoms should not automatically be attributed to psoriasis.

What perianal psoriasis can look like

Perianal means around the anus. Psoriasis here often produces clearly defined, shiny inflamed patches with little visible scale. The area may itch, burn, sting or develop small painful cracks, particularly when sweat, stool or friction irritates it.

The skin can look different from psoriasis on an elbow or knee because moisture and rubbing remove the surface scale. A lack of flaking therefore does not rule it out.

People with psoriasis elsewhere may develop symptoms in this area, but genital or perianal skin can also be the first place they notice it. Check with a clinician rather than trying to identify the condition from photographs.

Psoriasis is an inflammatory skin disease, not a sexually transmitted infection, and it cannot be passed to a partner by touch. This does not mean every genital rash in someone with psoriasis has the same cause.

Plaque psoriasis and inverse psoriasis can both involve this region. Inverse psoriasis particularly affects folds, including the groin, buttock crease and skin beneath the buttocks; nearby vulval, penile or scrotal skin may also be affected. This is additional involvement of an inflammatory condition, not infection spreading from one person to another.

Why an examination matters

Irritant or allergic dermatitis, fungal infection, anal fissures and other skin or bowel conditions can cause similar discomfort. A sexually transmitted infection may also need consideration depending on symptoms and exposure.

Tell the clinician when the problem began, whether you have bleeding or discharge, what happens during bowel movements and which creams or wipes you use. Mention psoriasis elsewhere and any treatment already tried.

An examination is often enough to guide the next step. In some cases a swab, skin scraping, allergy testing or biopsy is appropriate, especially if the appearance is unusual or the rash does not respond as expected. You can ask for a chaperone and an explanation before the examination.

Do not keep escalating a cream because the area still itches. Persistent symptoms may mean a different diagnosis, an additional infection or irritation from the treatment itself.

Treatment must suit this location

A dermatologist may prescribe a mild topical corticosteroid for a limited course, with clear instructions about the amount and review date. This skin absorbs medicines readily, so repeated unsupervised use of a strong steroid can cause harm.

Other prescribed options may include a non-steroid anti-inflammatory cream such as tacrolimus or pimecrolimus. The right choice depends on the diagnosis, local approvals and how the skin responds. Report burning or irritation that makes treatment difficult.

Do not reuse an elbow or scalp treatment here without checking. Retinoids, strong coal-tar preparations and other irritating products can be unsuitable. Keep externally prescribed creams outside the anal canal unless the clinician specifically instructs otherwise.

If symptoms remain severe, specialist systemic treatment may be considered even when the affected area is small. Quality of life matters alongside the amount of skin involved. Oral steroids are not a routine self-treatment for psoriasis.

Do not expose genital or perianal skin to home UV lamps or tanning beds. If you receive medical phototherapy for psoriasis elsewhere, follow the clinic’s instructions about shielding sensitive areas.

Reduce irritation during everyday care

Clean gently after bowel movements and pat dry rather than scrubbing. Avoid fragranced wipes, deodorants, antiseptics and repeated harsh washing. Ask about a suitable bland moisturiser or barrier preparation if stool or moisture is irritating the skin.

Wear comfortable clothing that reduces rubbing, and change out of damp or sweaty underwear. Try to avoid scratching, which can damage skin and make the discomfort worse.

If passing stool is painful or you are constipated, discuss ways to keep bowel movements comfortable. Do not assume a crack or bleeding is only a skin flare.

No special food has been shown to cure perianal psoriasis. If you notice a consistent irritant or trigger, record it for your appointment rather than removing many foods or starting restrictive diets.

Pause sexual activity that hurts or rubs broken skin. Discuss compatible lubricants and whether a prescribed product could affect condoms or transfer to a partner. Psoriasis itself is not contagious, and you deserve practical advice without embarrassment.

Stress, rubbing or injury and some medicines can coincide with a flare. Bring a medication list and any consistent trigger pattern to the visit, but do not stop treatment or assume every food is a trigger.

When to get help sooner

Arrange assessment for new bleeding, worsening pain, a persistent rash or symptoms that keep returning despite treatment. A history of psoriasis should not delay checking a different problem.

Seek urgent care for severe anal pain with fever, chills or feeling unwell, or for a painful swelling or pus that could indicate an abscess. Black or dark-red stool also needs urgent assessment.

Heavy or continuous rectal bleeding, large clots, faintness or collapse requires emergency care. These symptoms should not be managed simply by applying another layer of skin cream.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

AAD recommends a treatment plan specific to genital psoriasis, which may include carefully chosen topical therapy or specialist systemic treatment when symptoms are severe.

DermNet describes smooth anogenital psoriasis and competing diagnoses; persistent or unusual symptoms may need selective testing or biopsy.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you prepare questions about discomfort, bowel movements and treatment contact with sensitive skin. A clinician should confirm the diagnosis.

When to seek help

Severe anal pain with fever, swelling or pus needs urgent assessment. Heavy continuous bleeding, large clots, faintness or collapse requires emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Psoriasis around the anus may look shiny with little scale.
  • Other conditions can cause the same itching and pain.
  • Use a treatment prescribed for this sensitive location.
  • Fever, severe pain or significant bleeding needs prompt help.

Frequently asked questions

Can I have perianal psoriasis without patches elsewhere?

Yes, although an examination is needed because other rashes and anal conditions can look similar.

Is it an infection I can pass to a partner?

Psoriasis itself is not contagious. A new rash may still need tests to exclude an infection or another cause.

Can I use my usual strong psoriasis cream?

Check first. Genital and perianal skin need a location-specific plan, and some products used elsewhere can irritate or damage it.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
